page.text:
While differentiation examines instantaneous rates of change at a point,
*integration* performs the global synthesis: accumulating infinitesimal contributions
over a continuum to determine areas, volumes, total mass, and work.

Conceived in antiquity by Archimedes as the method of exhaustion and rigorized
in the nineteenth century by Bernhard Riemann and Gaston Darboux, integration
sandwiches a bounded function between upper and lower step functions determined
by finite partitions. A function is *Riemann integrable* when the supremum of its
lower Darboux sums coincides with the infimum of its upper Darboux sums:
$$ \underline{\int_a^b} f(x) \, dx = \overline{\int_a^b} f(x) \, dx = \int_a^b f(x) \, dx. $$
Integrability is thus a profound convergence theorem rather than a triviality
of notation.
